newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania polls may close early over security fears.
newsitem.headline: Albania polls may close early over security fears.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha said on Thursday he supported an early closing of polling stations in a general election on Sunday, clearing one of the last obstacles worrying international poll organisers.

The Organisation for Security and Coooperation in Europe (OSCE), overseeing the election, hundreds of observers and military leaders of a multinational protection force are concerned that lives could be put at risk if polling stations did not close before nightfall.

"There is no political question in this respect, only a legal one," Berisha told reporters after holding more than an hour of talks with OSCE special envoy Franz Vranitzky. "I will support any legal solution that will be found."

All Albanian political parties, including Berisha's dominant Democrats, and top officials of the Central Electoral Commission have called for polls to close earlier than the 9 p.m. time laid down in laws governing the electoral process.
Diplomatic sources said Berisha had indicated he would agree to polling stations being open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. The issue will now have to come before the constitutional court.
A constitutional court spokeswoman said judges had begun gathering around midday on Thursday but was unable to give any details of why they were meeting.

Vranitzky, a former Austrian chancellor, held talks with Socialist leader Fatos Nano and Democrat chairman Tritan Shehu on Wednesday and was to meet other officials before leaving Tirana on Friday morning.

Albania is still under a state of emergency and a curfew imposed after days of shooting and lawlessness in March when anarchy gripped the country in response to the collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes.

Around 1,500 people have since been killed, many of them in gangland feuds or by accidental shootings and ricochets as men try to show off their prowess in handling arms looted from police and army stores during the chaos.

In the Adriatic port of Vlore, where anti-government protests turned into open rebellion in March, supporters at a rightist rally were forced to seek refuge in a sports arena as rival gunmen shot at each other. Such violence has been a daily occurence in the town for the past three months.

The first round of the general election on Sunday was called in March to try to seek political stability after an interim coalition government led by Berisha's rivals, the Socialists, was set up to prepare for the polls.

The closing time of voting is a crucial issue in the former communist state because international observers want to be present in at least 90 key polling stations to monitor the count and prevent the widespread manipulation witnessed in last year's general election.
Berisha's Democrats won 122 of the 140 seats in parliament while the Socialists, Albania's second biggest party, and other opposition groups boycotted the poll.

The first shipment of ballot papers arrived in Tirana from Italy on Thursday on a military C-130 plane. Italian soldiers unloaded stacks of paper wrapped in plastic foil and placed them in delivery vans under the eye of armed guards.
Campaigning by the parties has been at best sporadic, with both Democrats and Socialists unable to hold rallies in areas in the grip of rival supporters.
But Berisha said despite the difficulties he would accept the results of the election if they were backed by the OSCE.
"I have always declared, and I will keep to it, that I will recognise the result of the elections that I fully respect," he told reporters.
Asked whether he was prepared to share power if opposition parties formed the next government, Berisha would only say: "I will continue in politics until the last day. I will not withdraw."
